Eigenvalues and singular values

Source: vignettes/spectral.Rmd
spectral.Rmd

Installation 

install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("gcol33/linop")

Installing linop installs one package. There are no Imports and no compiled code, so there is no toolchain to have working first. Matrix sits in Suggests and is used for sparse leaves and as_sparse().

R 4.4.0 or newer. The floor is set by crossprod() and tcrossprod(), which became S3 generic in R 4.4.0, and are what let one matrixOps method cover all three matrix products.

Two verbs

eigs() computes a few eigenpairs of a hermitian operator. svds() computes a few singular triplets of any operator. Both run against the action alone, and both hold ncv vectors rather than a matrix.

The 1D Laplacian has closed-form eigenvalues, which makes it the fixture to check against:

n <- 200
lap <- function(X) 2 * X - rbind(X[-1, , drop = FALSE], 0) - rbind(0, X[-n, , drop = FALSE])
L <- linop(lap, adjoint = lap, dim = c(n, n), properties = c(hermitian = TRUE))

truth <- 2 - 2 * cos(seq_len(n) * pi / (n + 1))

fit <- eigs(L, k = 3, which = "largest_algebraic", ncv = 60)
fit
#> <primme> 0 of 3 requested eigenpairs converged, which = 'largest_algebraic'
#>   300 iterations of at most 300, 9 restarts
#>   values: 3.999756  3.999023  3.997802
#>   certificate: fail
rbind(computed = fit$values,
      closed_form = rev(sort(truth))[1:3])
#>                 [,1]     [,2]     [,3]
#> computed    3.999756 3.999023 3.997802
#> closed_form 3.999756 3.999023 3.997802

The operator has to say it is hermitian

There is one eigensolver here and it is Lanczos, which is defined for a hermitian operator. Symmetry is not probed and not assumed:

Undeclared <- linop(lap, adjoint = lap, dim = c(n, n))
eigs(Undeclared, k = 2)
#> Error:
#> ! method 'eigs' requires the operator to be hermitian; it declares hermitian = NA.
#>   Unknown is not false. Declare it with linop(..., properties = c(hermitian = TRUE)) if you can justify it.

Unknown is not false, and the refusal says so rather than guessing either way. A dense leaf establishes symmetry by checking it, so a matrix needs no declaration; a callback has nothing to check and the declaration is how you supply it.

A non-hermitian operator is refused for a different reason, and there is no Arnoldi in this version, so it has no eigensolver here at all. svds() works on any operator and is often the thing that was actually wanted.

ncv is the knob that matters

ncv is how many vectors a restart holds. Each restart compresses the subspace to the vectors it keeps, so the smaller ncv is, the more applies the method spends reaching the tolerance:

ladder <- t(vapply(c(20, 30, 40, 60), function(nc) {
  f <- eigs(L, k = 3, which = "largest_algebraic", ncv = nc)
  c(ncv = nc,
    error = max(abs(f$values - rev(sort(truth))[1:3])),
    converged = f$nconv,
    applies = f$iterations)
}, numeric(4)))
ladder
#>      ncv        error converged applies
#> [1,]  20 2.040628e-09         0     302
#> [2,]  30 4.101608e-12         0     300
#> [3,]  40 2.620126e-14         0     301
#> [4,]  60 1.332268e-15         0     300

At ncv = 20 the default budget of 300 applies runs out before the residuals reach the tolerance, and the run reports the pairs it has as unconverged. A larger budget recovers it:

eigs(L, k = 3, which = "largest_algebraic", ncv = 20, maxit = 2000)$nconv
#> [1] 3

The top of the Laplacian’s spectrum is tightly clustered, which is what makes a small subspace slow here. A well-separated spectrum needs far fewer applies.

What gets reported is the Rayleigh quotient

The value attached to each vector is x^H A x / (x^H x), measured against A itself rather than read off the projected problem. It is the choice of mu that minimises ||A x - mu x||, so no other value certifies better for the vector that was found.

That matters most under a shift, where the projected problem is a solve against A - sigma I and its own accuracy is a separate question. Measuring on A means nothing downstream inherits the inner solve’s error.

Which end 

c(largest  = eigs(L, k = 2, which = "largest_algebraic",  ncv = 60)$values,
  smallest = eigs(L, k = 2, which = "smallest_algebraic", ncv = 40)$values)
#>     largest1     largest2    smallest1    smallest2 
#> 3.9997557139 3.9990229152 0.0002442861 0.0009770848

"largest" and "smallest" order by magnitude, "largest_algebraic" and "smallest_algebraic" by value. For an operator with a negative eigenvalue those are different questions. RSpectra’s "LM", "SM", "LA" and "SA" are accepted for the same four, so existing calling code ports without edits.

Eigenvalues near a point

A shift is the way to reach the interior of a spectrum. sigma runs the same recurrence on (A - sigma I)^-1, and that inverse is not formed: it is the package’s own solvers, applied once per step.

near <- eigs(L, k = 3, sigma = 0.01, ncv = 30, inner = list(method = "minres"))
rbind(computed = sort(near$values),
      closed_form = sort(truth[order(abs(truth - 0.01))][1:3]))
#>                   [,1]        [,2]       [,3]
#> computed    0.00610417 0.008788036 0.01195833
#> closed_form 0.00610417 0.008788036 0.01195833

inner carries the arguments for that solve, so its method and tolerance are yours to set. This is the one place the two halves of the package meet: everything in vignette("solvers") is available inside a spectral computation.

A shift is expensive, because each Lanczos step now costs a full linear solve. It is the right tool when the eigenvalues wanted are in the middle, where no amount of ncv will reach them directly.

Singular values

svds() needs both the forward action and the adjoint, and requires nothing else:

G <- matrix(rnorm(60 * 12), 60, 12)
R <- linop(G)

sv <- svds(R, k = 2)
rbind(computed = sv$d, closed_form = svd(G)$d[1:2])
#>                 [,1]     [,2]
#> computed    11.17144 10.08422
#> closed_form 11.17144 10.08422

The triplets satisfy what they should:

c(`A v - d u` = max(abs(G %*% sv$v - sv$u %*% diag(sv$d))),
  `U orthonormal` = max(abs(crossprod(sv$u) - diag(2))),
  `V orthonormal` = max(abs(crossprod(sv$v) - diag(2))))
#>     A v - d u U orthonormal V orthonormal 
#>  8.881784e-16  2.220446e-16  2.220446e-16

Underneath, this is eigs() on the hermitian augmented operator

H = [ 0    A  ]
    [ A^H  0  ]

whose eigenpairs are (sigma, [u; v]/sqrt(2)). H is hermitian for every A with nothing to declare, which is why svds() asks the operator for no properties where eigs() asks for one. One consequence is worth knowing: the certificate’s orthogonality row measures the augmented basis, where a deviation in U could cancel one in V, so the check above measures the two separately.

which = "smallest" is accepted and is the hard end of the problem. A Krylov space reaches the largest singular values first, so the smallest need a subspace approaching the rank of the operator:

small <- svds(R, k = 2, which = "smallest", ncv = 12)
rbind(computed = small$d, closed_form = rev(svd(G)$d)[1:2])
#>                 [,1]     [,2]
#> computed    4.746325 5.603087
#> closed_form 4.746325 5.603087

The request is not refused. What was reached is reported, and the certificate is where you find out whether it was enough.

A result that is right and certifies as fail

This is worth meeting once, because it looks like a bug and is not:

smallest <- eigs(L, k = 3, which = "smallest_algebraic", ncv = 40)

rbind(computed = smallest$values, closed_form = sort(truth)[1:3])
#>                     [,1]         [,2]        [,3]
#> computed    0.0002442861 0.0009770848 0.002198217
#> closed_form 0.0002442861 0.0009770848 0.002198217
smallest$certificate$overall
#> [1] "fail"

Every value is right to the last printed digit and the certificate says fail. The reason is in which row failed:

smallest$certificate
#> solved by primme (hermitian operator, PRIMME with implicit restarting (highest priority))
#> ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#> check                          status       source           guarantee             conf
#> ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#> arithmetic floor               pass         computation      estimate              -
#> residual                       fail         computation      estimate              -
#> orthogonality                  pass         computation      identity              1
#> backward error                 fail         computation      estimate              -
#> target identity                not_checked  computation      identity              -
#> convergence                    fail         computation      identity              1
#> forward error                  fail         theorem          deterministic_bound   1
#> ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#> overall                        fail   no deterministic bound on: arithmetic floor, residual, backward error, target identity
#> 
#> failures:
#>   residual: worst ||A x - theta x|| / (|theta| ||x||) = 9.145e-05 against tol 1.000e-10, floor 1.450e-11
#>   backward error: worst ||A x - theta x|| / (||A|| ||x||) = 2.241e-08 against tol 1.000e-10
#>   convergence: 0 of 3 requested pairs converged in 301 of at most 300 iterations; budget exhausted
#>   forward error: min_j |theta - lambda_j(A)| <= 8.936e-08, that is 2.241e-08 relative to ||A||; the eigenvectors are not covered, which needs a certified separation and not a Ritz gap

backward error passes at 1.4e-13 and forward error, which is a real bound here, passes at 5.2e-13. What failed is residual, which divides by |theta|, and the smallest eigenvalue of this operator is 2.4e-4. A residual sitting near the arithmetic floor is still large relative to a tiny eigenvalue.

overall is a summary of seven rows, and each row answers its own question. The rows are what to read. vignette("certificates") covers what each one measures.
